extracted.intended_audience: creative writers, screenwriters, literature and film students, and readers studying narrative techniques
extracted.subtask_short: using in medias res in storytelling
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for employing (or identifying) the 'in medias res' narrative technique — beginning a story in the chronological middle and revealing earlier events later. Covers literary and cinematic uses, historical origins, purposes, and common methods for supplying backstory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begins in the chronological middle (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrative opens in the chronological middle of the plot, rather than at the beginning (cf. ab ovo / ab initio).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the defining criterion for labeling a work 'in medias res'; compare to stories that start at origins. Examples: Hamlet begins after the death of Hamlet's father; the Iliad opens during the Trojan War rather than at its start.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bypass initial exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposition is initially bypassed instead of being presented at the story's start.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors can avoid lengthy set‑up and begin with an engaging present moment; the missing background is later supplied gradually. Shakespeare uses this to bypass superfluous exposition when the play's focus is action rather than motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fill in backstory gradually (dialogue, flashbacks, description)
rubrics_metrics.description: Background information and earlier events are revealed incrementally through dialogue, flashbacks, or descriptive passages rather than up front.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common techniques to supply the skipped exposition include character dialogue, flashback sequences, and descriptive recounting of past events. Example: The Odyssey reveals most of Odysseus's earlier journey in Books IX–XII after the narrative has already begun.

rubrics_metrics.name: Later use of flashback and nonlinear narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Works that begin in medias res often employ flashback or nonlinear structures later to provide exposition and context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan the narrative so later flashbacks or nonlinear segments satisfactorily fill in essential backstory; Homer's Odyssey and many modern novels follow this pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize action over motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use in medias res when the story's central concern is immediate action or event rather than the origins or motivations leading up to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the plot's primary interest is what happens (e.g., revenge, combat), opening in the middle can focus reader attention on the action. Example: Hamlet’s play centers on the revenge plot; motivation is referenced rather than fully established at the start.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horace's directive: 'hurry to the action'
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical guidance (Horace, Ars Poetica): do not begin from the very origin; hurry to the action and snatch the listener into the middle of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prescriptive stance supports starting at an engaging moment rather than an exhaustive origin story — a classical justification for in medias res in epic and poetic composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for epic and oral traditions
rubrics_metrics.description: In medias res is a stylistic convention with likely origins in oral tradition and is characteristic of epic poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The technique fits oral/epic storytelling where narrators may begin at an eventful point and rely on later narration to supply earlier events. Exemplars include Homer’s Iliad and Odyssey and the Mahābhārata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cinematic use: begin with incident, reveal via investigation/flashback (film noir example)
rubrics_metrics.description: In film, especially film noir, narratives often open with a crime or dramatic incident already in progress; the backstory is revealed through investigation or flashbacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach creates immediate intrigue and lets the audience piece together events as characters uncover them. Examples: Crossfire (1947) opens with a murder then explains the story via investigation and flashback; Dead Reckoning (1947) begins with the protagonist on the run and supplies backstory through explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use across cinematic genres to create immediacy and tension
rubrics_metrics.description: In medias res appears in many film genres (drama, crime thrillers, horror, action, comedy) to open with a compelling moment and then provide context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directors use it to heighten immediacy, suspense, or comic effect; examples span Through a Glass Darkly, The Usual Suspects, Raging Bull, Kill Bill Volume 2, Dr. Strangelove, Star Wars (argued), and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animated-film variant: brief foreshadowing scene revisited
rubrics_metrics.description: Animated films sometimes open with a short but significant scene that foreshadows earlier events; that scene is later shown again or recontextualized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This variant gives an early hook and later payoff when the viewer sees the fuller context. Examples: Grave of the Fireflies, The Emperor's New Groove, Hoodwinked!, Megamind, The Mitchells vs. the Machines.

rubrics_metrics.name: War films: start with combat to convey immediacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Many war films begin in medias res with protagonists already in combat, foregoing prior domestic or origin scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opening in action places the audience immediately into the stakes and chaos of war; example: The Thin Red Line (1998).

rubrics_metrics.name: Biographical/narrative nonfiction: start with a turning point
rubrics_metrics.description: Some biographies and nonfiction narratives begin with a pivotal moment in the subject's life rather than chronological origins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Starting at a turning point can engage readers and then allow the narrative to fill in earlier life events; example: David McCullough’s Truman begins with his World War I experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing/informal metadata: relation to related techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: In medias res is related to other narrative devices such as cold open, flashforward, and reverse chronology and can be used as a framing device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider alternative or complementary devices (cold open, flashforward) when choosing how to structure beginning and exposition; combining techniques can produce varied effects depending on tone and genre.
